newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Five hurt in clash near APEC summit venue.
newsitem.headline: Five hurt in clash near APEC summit venue.

text.p: At least five people were injured on Monday when supporters and foes of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum clashed near the APEC summit venue, witnesses said.

Police detained one person after breaking up the fight which erupted outside a public market in the town of Olongapo, just outside Subic Bay where U.S. President Bill Clinton and leaders of 17 other APEC member economies were holding their annual summit.

The clash occurred after thousands of leftist protesters who had travelled by motor cavalcade from Manila decided in nearby Dinalupihan town to call off their planned march into Subic Bay rather than risk confrontation with riot police.
Four of the injured were treated for cuts in their heads in an Olongapo hospital. The staff said they were pro-APEC supporters.
A fifth man who also suffered cuts was taken in by police for questioning. Police said the man was an officer of a leftist group opposed to APEC.
Opponents of APEC say developing countries are not ready for the rigours of free trade that APEC advocates, and they fear rising unemployment.

Witnesses said the clash occurred when the two groups, numbering a few dozen, ran into each other near the public market. In the scuffle, the anti-APEC protesters grabbed the placards of the pro group and struck them with the sticks, according to the witnesses.

Elsewhere in Olongapo, 80 km (50 miles) north of Manila, another group of anti-APEC protesters were blocked by pro-APEC residents who carried placards reading, "If you want trouble, don't do it here." But there was no violence.
In Manila, police and troops in riot gear surrounded about 1,000 leftist demonstrators who had gathered in a city square for a protest march to the U.S. embassy.
The police were refusing to allow the protesters to march but there was no violence and some members of the security forces used their riot shields as shelters from the pouring rain.
In Dinalupihan, police blocked the highway leading to the summit venue with cargo trucks and fire engines to prevent an estimated 7,000 leftwing protesters from entering Olongapo.

"Considering the large number of our enemy, we will not sacrifice our bodies, we will not sacrifice our force because that will be suicide," leftist leader Nathaniel Santiago told protesters assembled at Dinalupihan, about 20 km (12 miles) from the summit venue.
"We will no longer continue," chief rally organiser Satur Ocampo told reporters.
"We are realistic enough to recognise that we cannot break through this last barricade," he added, referring to columns of police and the trucks blocking the protesters' path.
Most of the protesters drove into Dinalupihan in convoy, braving heat and rain, enduring hunger and defying numerous police blocks that slowed down the cavalcade.
Many rode in distinctive "jeepneys" -- colourful minibuses modelled on World War Two jeeps -- flying streamers with slogans slamming APEC.
Regional police chief General Edgardo Aglipay told reporters he had about 2,000 police ready to stop the cavalcade and added: "It's up to them if they kill us."
